To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the professionalisation of early childhood education (ECE) in Aotearoa, New Zealand has led to unintended consequences that include the loss of children's free play, the prioritisation of safety over exploration, the use of surveillance as an accountability measure and the commodification of children as an investment.

the unintended consequences of early childhood education in Aotearo/New Zealand have resulted in a focus on children as an investment, which has led to the commodification of children and a focus on accountability and surveillance.
the early childhood sector's professionalisation is a double-edged sword.
In summary, our research is concerned with

how the early childhood sector has become increasingly 'institutionalised' (Merton, 1936) and how this may be affecting the sector's capacity to support children's 'free' play and 'free' exploration (Bunkle 1995).

how the early childhood sector in Aotearo/New Zealand has been shaped by the 'unintended consequences' of professionalisation and how these have been shaped by the sector's own history, its relationship with the wider education sector, and its relationship with the state.
how early childhood education in Aotearoa, New Zealand has become a sector of 'odd alliances', and what this means for the children and families we work with.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the professionalisation of the sector has led to the 'normalisation' of children's experiences.
early childhood education is a complex, dynamic, contested, and often contradictory sector.
early childhood education is a sector in which the professionalisation process has been so successful that the sector is now at risk of becoming a victim of its own success.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the professionalisation of the sector has been accompanied by a 'normalisation' of children.
the sector has been pushed to focus on the needs of adults rather than children and that the sector's professional status has been compromised by a focus on accountability rather than quality.
early childhood education has become a 'hot commodity' in New Zealand.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the sector's professional identity, and the discourses that support it, are not always in alignment with the sector's values.
unintended consequences are not always negative, but that the sector must remain vigilant in its commitment to children's wellbeing.
the early childhood sector has been shaped by the unintended consequences of the professionalisation process.
